title: Indian Weavers
author: Sarojini Naidu
summary: In this short lyric Sarojini Naidu, the 'Nightingale of India', shows weavers weaving cloth for three stages of human life — birth, marriage (youth) and death. Each stanza matches a time of day, a colour and an occasion, so the poem is about the whole cycle of life. It is written as questions and answers between the poet and the weavers.

At 'break of day' (dawn) the poet asks why they weave a garment so 'gay' (bright and cheerful). The weavers say they weave the robes of a new-born child, blue as the wing of a wild halcyon (kingfisher). Morning, the beginning of the day, matches birth, the beginning of life; blue suggests freshness and hope.

At 'fall of night' (evening) they weave a bright garment like the plumes (feathers) of a peacock, purple and green — the marriage veils of a queen. Evening matches youth and the joy of marriage; purple and green suggest royalty and celebration.

Now the weavers work 'solemn and still' in the 'moonlight chill'. The poet asks what they weave; they reply that they weave a dead man's funeral shroud, white as a feather and white as a cloud. The cold, silent night matches the end of life; white stands for peace and purity.

Similes: 'blue as the wing of halcyon wild', 'like the plumes of a peacock', 'white as a feather and white as a cloud'. Imagery of colour and time; rhyme in couplets (day/gay, wild/child, night/bright, green/queen, still/chill, cloud/shroud). The mood changes from joyful to solemn. The poem celebrates the skill of Indian weavers and shows the cycle of life — birth, youth and death.

sa2: For whom do the weavers weave at break of day and in the moonlight chill?
At break of day they weave robes for a new-born child; in the moonlight chill they weave a funeral shroud for a dead man.
What are the weavers weaving at break of day?
They are weaving the bright blue robes of a new-born child, blue as the wing of a wild halcyon.
What is the similarity between 'break of day' and 'a new-born child'?
Both stand for a beginning: dawn is the beginning of the day and birth is the beginning of life; both are fresh and full of hope.
Why are the weavers 'solemn and still' at night?
They are weaving a funeral shroud for a dead man; death is a sad, serious occasion, so their mood is quiet and solemn.
What three stages of life are shown in the poem?
Birth (robes of a new-born child), youth/marriage (marriage veils of a queen) and death (a dead man's funeral shroud).
sa3: How does the poet link the time of day, colour and occasion in 'Indian Weavers'?

At break of day (beginning) the weavers weave blue robes for a new-born child (birth). At fall of night they weave bright purple and green marriage veils for a queen (youth and joy). In the moonlight chill they weave a white funeral shroud (death). Time, colour and mood together show the cycle of life.

or: Pick out the similes in 'Indian Weavers' and explain any two.

'Blue as the wing of halcyon wild', 'like the plumes of a peacock, purple and green', 'white as a feather and white as a cloud'. The first compares the child's robe to the bright blue kingfisher's wing, suggesting freshness; the last compares the shroud's whiteness to a feather and a cloud, suggesting peace, purity and lightness of the departing soul.
